metadata.title: Writing Hookify Rules
metadata.purpose: Answer whether stopping Claude from running a dangerous command needs custom code, using the writing-rules skill's own rm -rf block as the concrete case. Lands the carry-out that a hookify rule is a markdown file Claude reads before every tool call, not a script -- and it only catches exactly what its pattern says.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (the hookify rule blocking rm -rf: fires reliably at the exact pattern, then either over-fires on a broad pattern or lets a rephrased danger through on a narrow one)

beats.narration_text: Someone wants Claude to catch a dangerous command automatically. Their first thought: write a script. But hookify needs no code — just a rule. So: how do you write one that blocks rm -rf?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'How do I write a script to stop Claude from running rm -rf?', hesitates on 'script', corrects to 'rule', lands the real question

props.text:
How do I write a script
to stop Claude
from running rm -rf?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('script' -> 'rule') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: A hookify rule isn't code — it's a markdown file. Save it at dot-claude slash hookify dot name dot local dot md, with a YAML frontmatter block on top and a message underneath. There's no build step and no restart: Claude reads the file fresh on every single tool call, so an edit takes effect on the very next one.

shot.new_visual_element: A script/gears card receding while a markdown file card with a frontmatter divider grows in its place; the file path underneath; a 'read fresh, every call' tag

production_viz.label: A rule, not a script
production_viz.mechanic: Left: a card labelled 'custom hook script' with a terminal glyph, fading back. Right: a card labelled 'hookify rule' growing, showing a '---' frontmatter divider and two lines of YAML appearing beneath it. Below both, the file path '.claude/hookify.block-rm.local.md' fades in, then a small looping-arrows glyph with the words 'read fresh, every call'.

beats.narration_text: Five frontmatter fields sit above the message: name, kebab-case verb-first; enabled, true or false; event — bash, file, stop, prompt, or all; and pattern, a regex to match. Action defaults to warn; block stops the operation outright. Watch the anchor: event bash, pattern matching rm -rf, action block — Claude reaches for the command, the pattern matches, and it never runs.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — five field chips lighting in turn, then a rule card (event: bash / pattern: rm -rf / action: block), a command attempt arrowing into it, BLOCKED lighting in terracotta

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — five fields, then a block
production_viz.mechanic: Five small chips fade in one at a time across the top, each labelled with a field name (name / enabled / event / pattern / action), then fade out together. THE ANCHOR. A rule card appears centered: three stacked lines 'event: bash', 'pattern: rm -rf', 'action: block'. A command box reading 'rm -rf ~' arrows into the rule card; the rule card's text recolors to terracotta and a 'BLOCKED' chip lights beneath it. THIS EXACT SEQUENCE RETURNS AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Get that pattern exact and the block fires every time — reliable, because the check is a straight regex match. But precision cuts both ways. Pattern the word log, and you also catch catalog and login — blocking things nobody asked about. Pattern only rm -rf slash tmp, and the identical danger typed against a different path sails straight through.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — the same rule blocking three times in a row; then split: 'log' lighting up catalog/login as a false block, 'rm -rf /tmp' letting 'rm -rf ~' pass as a false miss

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — precision cuts both ways
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 RULE CARD RETURNS, identical, firing 'BLOCKED' three times in a row against three attempts. Then it splits into two cards side by side: left reads 'pattern: log' with 'catalog' and 'login' lighting up terracotta beneath it, labelled 'false block'; right reads 'pattern: rm -rf /tmp' with 'rm -rf ~' passing through unlit, labelled 'false miss'. A closing line beneath both: 'same match, opposite mistake'.

beats.narration_text: A hookify rule isn't a script you write — it's a markdown file Claude reads before every tool call, and it only catches exactly what its pattern says, no more, no less.

props.quote: A hookify rule isn't a script you write — it's a markdown file Claude reads before every tool call, and it only catches exactly what its pattern says, no more, no less.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Create a hookify rule that blocks rm -rf commands, and one that warns when editing .env files. Watch two things when Claude answers. Does the rm rule set action to block, not warn — warn still lets the command run. And does the .env rule check file_path directly, in a conditions block, rather than only the new text being written — a path check catches the edit itself, not just what's typed inside it. Liam, in for Bear.

props.command: Create a hookify rule that blocks rm -rf commands, and one that warns when editing .env files.
